title: T1021.006 — Remote Services: Windows Remote Management
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: Windows Remote Management with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.

steps.title: One password, many doors
steps.caption: WinRM is the built-in remote management service of Windows, and PowerShell Remoting runs on top of it. It is enabled by default on servers. The night starts with credential theft: the attacker now holds the password of a domain admin. One password can open many doors.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Ask who is listening on 5985
steps.caption: Before touching anything, the attacker asks if WinRM is listening. Test-WSMan sends a small WS-Management probe to TCP 5985 and needs no password. The server answers, so the listener is alive. Defenders would see a network connection from a workstation to a port that workstations rarely touch.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Open a remote PowerShell
steps.caption: The attacker opens a remote PowerShell session with the stolen password. On the server this is a Type 3 network logon, not a desktop logon. Windows starts wsmprovhost.exe to host the remote commands. That process is the key artifact: outside jump servers, it means someone is remoting in.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Run an encoded command everywhere
steps.caption: One command, many servers, in seconds. Invoke-Command copies the script to every computer in the list and runs it there. This one dumps LSASS memory with a signed Microsoft DLL, so no attacker file ever lands on disk. Only the script block log and the process events reveal it.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Pivot to the domain controller
steps.caption: Owning one server is not enough, so the attacker moves again. From APP-SRV-02 they run PowerShell Remoting against DC01 and create a new account called backup_svc. This is persistence: a way back in even if the stolen password is reset. On a domain controller, a new account always deserves a question.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Collect from the file server
steps.caption: The valuable files sit on the file server. The attacker mounts the Finance share from APP-SRV-02 and copies it with robocopy, a normal Windows tool. The traffic flows between two trusted servers, so it looks routine. Share access events and SMB connections are the traces to collect.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Try to look normal
steps.caption: The attacker wants the new account and the copies forgotten. From the remote PowerShell on DC01 they clear the Security event log. But clearing is itself a loud event, ID 1102, and it cannot be undone. A clean Security log on a domain controller is a red flag, not a relief.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: How defenders catch this
steps.caption: The attacker was fast, but the telemetry was faster. One rule pages the on-call analyst: wsmprovhost.exe on servers nobody remotes into, all from one workstation. The encoded command and the log clearing confirm the story. Within minutes the team disables the account and isolates the servers.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.
